claim: An estimated 3-4 million individuals become newly infected with hepatitis C virus (HCV) every year.
source: Every year, an estimated 3–4 million individuals become newly infected with hepatitis C virus (HCV) (Westbrook and Dusheiko, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Westbrook and Dusheiko, 2014.

claim: 60-80% of HCV-infected individuals go on to develop chronic infection.
source: Every year, an estimated 3–4 million individuals become newly infected with hepatitis C virus (HCV) (Westbrook and Dusheiko, 2014), with 60–80% going on to join the population of approximately 71.1 million who are chronically infected (Blach et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blach et al., 2017.

claim: Approximately 71.1 million people are chronically infected with HCV.
source: Every year, an estimated 3–4 million individuals become newly infected with hepatitis C virus (HCV) (Westbrook and Dusheiko, 2014), with 60–80% going on to join the population of approximately 71.1 million who are chronically infected (Blach et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blach et al., 2017.

claim: HCV has only been shown to robustly infect human and chimpanzee hepatocytes in vivo.
source: A hepatotropic virus, HCV has only been shown to robustly infect in vivo human and chimpanzee hepatocytes.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about HCV host tropism.

claim: The limited host tropism of HCV has hindered the development of an immunocompetent animal model.
source: This limited host tropism has proven problematic in developing an animal model that is not only ethically and financially sound but also immunocompetent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the restricted host range of HCV and the challenges in developing animal models.

claim: Human CD81 and human OCLN are the minimal factors needed for HCV viral entry into murine cells.
source: Of these, human CD81 and human OCLN were the minimal factors needed for viral entry (Ploss et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ploss et al., 2009.

claim: HCV adapted to utilize murine CD81 can overcome the entry barrier in murine cells.
source: Alternatively, infecting with HCV adapted to utilize murine CD81 could also successfully overcome this initial obstacle (Bitzegeio et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bitzegeio et al., 2010.

claim: HCV faces a block at the level of replication in murine cells.
source: Once inside murine cells, HCV faces another block at the level of replication, which initial studies circumvented through the use of selectable subgenomic HCV replicons (McCaffrey et al., 2002; Park et al., 2009; Uprichard et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McCaffrey et al., 2002; Park et al., 2009; Uprichard et al., 2006.

claim: Murine cells support HCV assembly and release of infectious particles at low levels when NS2 and structural HCV proteins are provided in trans and ApoE is overexpressed.
source: Murine cells did appear to support assembly and release of infectious particles, albeit at low levels, once NS2 and the structural HCV proteins were provided in trans and the murine or human ortholog of the apolipoprotein ApoE was overexpressed (Long et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Long et al., 2011.

claim: Disruption of innate immune responses improves HCV replication in murine cells.
source: Further efforts to improve HCV replication in a murine context have relied on disruption of innate immune responses (Aly et al., 2011; Anggakusuma et al., 2015; Chang et al., 2006; Frentzen et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2010; Nandakumar et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Robust HCV replication and completion of the life cycle following infection in murine cells is difficult unless a selectable genome is used.
source: with robust replication and completion of the HCV life cycle proving difficult following infection unless a selectable genome is used (Vogt et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vogt et al., 2013.

claim: Poor levels of HCV replication in murine cells could be due to lower compatibility of murine orthologs of vital replication host factors with the viral replication machinery.
source: These poor levels of replication could be due to the lower compatibility of murine orthologs of vital replication host factors with the viral replication machinery or the absence of proteins that normally facilitate these interactions in human cells.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Three host factors have extensive experimental evidence for their role in HCV replication: cyclophilin A (CypA), phosphatidylinositol four kinase IIIα (PI4KA), and microRNA-122 (miR-122).
source: Although numerous intracellular host factors have been implicated in HCV replication, extensive experimental evidence has only been provided for three host factors: cyclophilin A (CypA) (Kaul et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2008a), phosphatidylinositol four kinase IIIα (PI4KA) (Berger et al., 2009; Borawski et al., 2009; Reiss et al., 2011; Tai et al., 2009; Trotard et al., 2009) and microRNA-122 (miR-122) (Jopling et al., 2005; Lanford et al., 2010; Machlin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations for each factor.

claim: miR-122 is highly conserved between humans and mice.
source: miR-122 is highly conserved between humans and other species, including mice, making its expression alone unlikely to explain the weak replication of HCV in murine cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about miR-122 conservation.

claim: CypA is a cytosolic 18 kDa peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase (PPIase).
source: CypA is a cytosolic 18 kDa peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase (PPIase) and a part of the biologically ubiquitous cyclophilin enzyme family (Fischer et al., 1989)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fischer et al., 1989.

claim: CypA binds the immunosuppressive drug cyclosporin A (CsA).
source: the members of which were first characterized in mammals by their common ability to bind the immunosuppressive drug cyclosporin A (CsA) and their shared cyclophilin-like domain (CLD) which catalyzes the cis-trans isomerization of proline residues (reviewed in Marks, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marks, 1996.

claim: CypA overexpression has been implicated in various human diseases including cancer and atherosclerosis.
source: CypA overexpression has been implicated in a wide variety of human diseases, ranging from cancer to atherosclerosis (reviewed in Nigro et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nigro et al., 2013.

claim: CypA has a demonstrated role in the life cycles of multiple viruses besides HCV.
source: and it has a demonstrated role in the life cycles of multiple viruses besides HCV (de Wilde et al., 2018; Frausto et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016; Phillips et al., 2015; Tian et al., 2010; von Hahn and Ciesek, 2015; Watashi and Shimotohno, 2007; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CsA has an inhibitory effect on HCV in chronically infected chimpanzees.
source: Early work showed that CsA had an inhibitory effect on HCV in chronically infected chimpanzees
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge from early HCV research.

claim: CypA was recognized as critical to HCV replication through CypA knockdown experiments and dose-response assays with CsA derivatives.
source: but it was not until subsequent in vitro CypA knockdown experiments and dose-response assays with CsA derivatives that CypA was specifically recognized as critical to HCV replication (Chatterji et al., 2009; Ciesek et al., 2009; Coelmont et al., 2009; Kaul et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2009b; Yang et al., 2008b).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CypA's relevance to HCV replication is linked to its PPIase activity.
source: These studies showed that CypA's relevance to HCV replication was intimately linked to its PPIase activity, as the introduction of point mutations in the PPIase active site led to impaired viral replication (Chatterji et al., 2009; Kaul et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2009b).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Individuals with homozygosity at any of three SNP sites in the CypA coding region exhibit an HCV non-permissive phenotype.
source: Individuals exhibiting an HCV non-permissive phenotype were shown to express a rare homozygosity at any of three SNP sites in the coding region of CypA – but not in the enzymatic active site – that subsequent in vitro work showed resulted in markedly decreased levels of intracellular CypA (von Hahn et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to von Hahn et al., 2012.

claim: CypA interacts with HCV NS5B.
source: Interactions between CypA and several HCV proteins have been demonstrated, including the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) NS5B (Chatterji et al., 2009; Fernandes et al., 2007; Robida et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2008b)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CypA interacts with HCV NS5A.
source: NS5A (Anderson et al., 2011; Coelmont et al., 2010; Foster et al., 2011; Grisé et al., 2012; Hanoulle et al., 2009; Nag et al., 2012; Verdegem et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CypA interacts with HCV NS2.
source: and NS2 (Ciesek et al., 2009; Kaul et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ciesek et al., 2009 and Kaul et al., 2009.

claim: Human, chimpanzee, bonobo, gorilla, olive baboon, and rhesus macaque CypA are 100% identical at the amino acid level.
source: Human, chimpanzee, bonobo, gorilla, olive baboon, and rhesus macaque CypA are 100% identical at the amino acid level and for subsequent experiments the human CypA (hCypA) CDS was used as the representative sequence for these six species.
evidence: This is based on amino acid sequence alignment data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pigtailed macaques are predominantly homozygous for an insertion of the CypA exon at the TRIM5 locus, resulting in a chimeric TRIM5-CypA transcript.
source: Multiple studies have shown that pigtailed macaques are predominantly homozygous for an insertion of the CypA exon at the TRIM5 locus, resulting in a chimeric TRIM5-CypA transcript (Brennan et al., 2008; Liao et al., 2007; Newman et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Several non-human primate species appear resistant to HCV infection in vivo.
source: As observed in mice, previous in vivo studies have suggested that several non-human primate (NHP) species – including cynomolgus, Japanese, and rhesus macaque; African green monkey; and Chacma and doguera baboons – appear resistant to HCV infection (Abe et al., 1993; Bukh et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abe et al., 1993 and Bukh et al., 2001.

claim: Primary hepatocytes from rhesus macaques can support the HCV life cycle in vitro.
source: In contrast, more recent work in vitro demonstrated that primary hepatocytes from rhesus macaques (PRMH) (Scull et al., 2015) as well as hepatocyte-like cells derived from pigtailed macaque induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) could support the HCV life cycle (Sourisseau et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Scull et al., 2015.

claim: Hepatocyte-like cells derived from pigtailed macaque iPSCs can support the HCV life cycle.
source: In contrast, more recent work in vitro demonstrated that primary hepatocytes from rhesus macaques (PRMH) (Scull et al., 2015) as well as hepatocyte-like cells derived from pigtailed macaque induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) could support the HCV life cycle (Sourisseau et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sourisseau et al., 2013.

claim: Pharmacological-mediated suppression of innate immune responses via Jak inhibition enhances HCV replication in rhesus macaque primary hepatocytes.
source: Importantly, pharmacological-mediated suppression of innate immune responses via Jak inhibition enhanced viral replication in PRMH (Scull et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Scull et al., 2015.

claim: Tree shrews have been demonstrated as a potential platform for studying HCV infection.
source: Additionally, albeit with limited evidence, tree shrews have also been demonstrated as a potential platform for studying HCV infection (Amako et al., 2010; Tong et al., 2011; Xie et al., 1998; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Orangutan CypA differs from human CypA by a single amino acid.
source: Of the orthologs tested, only orangutan CypA, which differs from human CypA by a single amino acid, was capable of rescuing HCV replication at levels similar to human.
evidence: This is based on amino acid sequence alignment and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Orangutan CypA can rescue HCV replication at levels similar to human CypA.
source: Of the orthologs tested, only orangutan CypA, which differs from human CypA by a single amino acid, was capable of rescuing HCV replication at levels similar to human.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Mouse CypA can facilitate HCV replication but at levels ~3-4% of those observed for human CypA.
source: Compared to human CypA (normalized to 100%), mouse CypA could still facilitate HCV replication but at levels ~3–4% of those observed for human, that is ca. 30-fold decrease.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Tree shrew CypA did not significantly increase HCV replication above the levels observed in parental Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells.
source: Tupaia CypA, which was well expressed by western blot, did not significantly increase HCV replication above the levels observed in the parental Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Six amino acids differ between murine and human CypA.
source: Thus, still in a human context, we sought to determine how the six amino acid differences between murine and human CypA contributed to the decreased ability of murine CypA to facilitate HCV replication in Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells.
evidence: This is based on amino acid sequence alignment data presented in Figure 2a.

claim: None of the six amino acid differences between human and mouse CypA fall in the CsA-binding site.
source: None of these differences fell in the CsA-binding site of CypA (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Human CypA is more sensitive to single amino acid changes than mouse CypA, with significant decreases in rescue efficiency for all single residue changes tested.
source: Human CypA was more sensitive to changes in the amino acid sequence, with significant decreases in rescue efficiency for all single residue changes tested (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Humanizing residues 12, 14, 52, or 76 in mouse CypA results in levels of HCV replication comparable to those observed with human CypA.
source: Mouse CypA demonstrated a greater ability to facilitate HCV replication, at least in a human cell context, when either residues 12, 14, 52 or 76 were altered, with levels of replication comparable to those observed in the presence of human CypA (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Triply humanized murine CypA (T11A/A12V/D14G) can rescue HCV replication at levels comparable to human CypA.
source: Indeed, we observed a striking reversal of phenotype for both constructs, with 'humanized' murine CypA able to rescue HCV replication at levels comparable to human and vice versa for 'murinized' human CypA (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Triply murinized human CypA (A11T/V12A/G14D) shows decreased ability to rescue HCV replication compared to wild-type human CypA.
source: Indeed, we observed a striking reversal of phenotype for both constructs, with 'humanized' murine CypA able to rescue HCV replication at levels comparable to human and vice versa for 'murinized' human CypA (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Murine CypA does not exhibit a dominant negative effect on HCV replication.
source: The presence of elevated human CypA along with murine CypA in the same cells did not result in a significant decline in infection, indicating no dominant negative effect.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Triply humanized murine CypA supports HCV spread and release of infectious particles as efficiently as human CypA.
source: At three and five dpi, viral spread was assessed by NS5A staining (Figure 5b), which significantly increased over time only for the +human CypA and +triply humanized mouse CypA cultures.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5b and 5c.

claim: Clone 8 cells demonstrate sustained de novo HCV replication compared to parental Hep56.1D cells.
source: These so-called Clone 8 cells demonstrated sustained de novo replication compared to the parental Hep56.1D cells, regardless of whether mApoE was present.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Addition of murine CypA to Clone 8 cells results in increased HCV replication.
source: Addition of murine CypA resulted in a further increase in replication that was even greater for human CypA.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Addition of human CypA to Clone 8 cells results in greater HCV replication than murine CypA.
source: Addition of murine CypA resulted in a further increase in replication that was even greater for human CypA.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Infectious particle production in Clone 8 cells is not significantly greater than in parental Hep56.1D cells despite elevated replication and presence of mApoE.
source: In spite of the elevated replication and presence of mApoE in our Clone 8 cells, infectious particle production was not even a log greater than the parental Hep56.1D cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: In the United States, there has been a more than 133% increase in acute HCV incidence over the past decade, strongly associated with the domestic opioid epidemic.
source: In the United States alone over the past decade, there has been a more than 133% increase in acute HCV incidence, which is strongly associated with the domestic opioid epidemic (Zibbell et al., 2018; Zibbell et al., 2014; Zibbell et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Zibbell et al.

claim: Reinfection with HCV can occur after treatment and is likely among high-risk individuals such as injection drug users and HIV-positive men who have sex with men.
source: Even with treatment, which has its own financial and logistical limitations, reinfection can still occur and is likely among high-risk individuals such as injection drug users and HIV-positive men who have sex with men (Falade-Nwulia and Sulkowski, 2017; Hill et al., 2017; Salazar-Vizcaya et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CypA stably binds NS5A and this interaction is dependent on the protein's PPIase activity.
source: CypA stably binds NS5A and this interaction is dependent on the protein's PPIase activity (Chatterji et al., 2010b)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chatterji et al., 2010b.

claim: CypA promotes the isomerization of multiple conserved proline residues in domains II and III of NS5A, contributing to the protein's proper folding.
source: which promotes the isomerization of multiple conserved proline residues in domains II and III of NS5A, contributing to the protein's proper folding (Coelmont et al., 2009; Foster et al., 2011; Grisé et al., 2012; Hanoulle et al., 2009; Verdegem et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CypA promotes the RNA-binding capacity of NS5A.
source: As with NS5B, CypA is also believed to promote the RNA-binding capacity of NS5A (Nag et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nag et al., 2012.

claim: Upon inhibition of CypA activity, lipid and protein trafficking patterns associated with the formation of lipid droplets and the VLDL synthesis pathway are altered.
source: Upon inhibition of CypA activity, lipid and protein trafficking patterns associated with the formation of lipid droplets and the VLDL synthesis pathway are altered (Anderson et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 2011.

claim: When CypA expression or PPIase activity is inhibited, formation of double membrane vesicles (DMVs) is abrogated.
source: Furthermore, whether CypA expression or just its PPIase activity is inhibited, formation of double membrane vesicles (DMVs) – a prevalent component of the membranous web derived from the host endoplasmic reticulum (ER) which serves as scaffolding for viral genome replication (Paul et al., 2013; Romero-Brey et al., 2012) – is abrogated (Chatterji et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chatterji et al., 2015.

claim: A portion of host CypA is localized to ER compartments.
source: A portion of host CypA is already localized to ER compartments, which could be advantageous for later HCV replication complex formation in these same regions (Chatterji et al., 2010a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chatterji et al., 2010a.

claim: Treatment of infected cells with cyclophilin inhibitors leads to changes in the ER that temporarily prevent re-infection.
source: Indeed, treatment of infected cells with cyclophilin inhibitors leads to changes in the ER that temporarily prevent re-infection (Chatterji et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chatterji et al., 2016.

claim: An interaction between CypA and NS2 has been suggested, possibly impacting the cleavage of NS2 from NS3 by the NS2-NS3 protease.
source: Finally, an interaction between CypA and the viral assembly factor and protease NS2 has also been suggested, perhaps impacting the cleavage of NS2 from NS3 by the NS2-NS3 protease (Ciesek et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ciesek et al., 2009.

claim: CypA may impact the overall proteolytic processing of the HCV polyprotein.
source: and/or the overall proteolytic processing of the HCV polyprotein (Kaul et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kaul et al., 2009.

claim: Mutations in NS5B are linked to CsA resistance.
source: A connection between CypA and the HCV RdRp is evidenced by mutations in NS5B linked to CsA resistance (Fernandes et al., 2007; Robida et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2008a)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: NS5B can bind at the CypA active site.
source: and indications that NS5B can bind at the CypA active site (Chatterji et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2008a)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chatterji et al., 2009 and Yang et al., 2008a.

claim: CypA binding to NS5B might enhance the viral protein's RNA-binding capacity.
source: which might enhance the viral protein's RNA-binding capcacity as a result (Nag et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nag et al., 2012.

claim: Mutations in domain 2 of NS5A are linked to CsA treatment resistance among patients.
source: Mutations specifically in domain 2 of NS5A were linked to CsA treatment resistance among patients (Goto et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Goto et al., 2009.

claim: The cluster of three residues (positions 11, 12, and 14) may play a role in maintaining interactions with the HCV replication machinery and/or associating with host factors that help facilitate such interactions.
source: This raises the intriguing possibility that this cluster of three residues plays a role in maintaining these interactions with the HCV replication machinery and/or associating with host factors that help facilitate such interactions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings.

claim: The location of the three residues (11, 12, 14) on the face of the protein opposite the CsA-binding/active site makes it unclear whether changing these residues leads to a loss of PPIase activity.
source: The location of the three residues on the face of the protein opposite the CsA-binding/active site makes it unclear whether changing these residues leads to a loss of PPIase activity that would explain the accompanying change in phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural modeling data.

claim: Replication of full-length HCV genomes following transfection in primary murine hepatocytes remained low unless MAVS, IRF1 or IFNAR were knocked out.
source: Similarly, replication of full-length HCV RNA following transfection in primary murine hepatocytes remained low unless MAVS, IRF1 or IFNAR — all important players in cell-intrinsic antiviral responses — were knocked out (Aly et al., 2011; Nandakumar et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aly et al., 2011 and Nandakumar et al., 2013.

claim: Transfecting full-length genomes into MAVS-/- MLT cells expressing miR-122 and human HCV entry factors results in robust replication and infectious particle production.
source: Transfecting full-length genomes into MAVS-/- MLT cells expressing miR-122 and the human HCV entry factors resulted in robust replication and infectious particle production; however, in performing infections, replication declined and infectious particle release fell below background levels (Frentzen et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Frentzen et al., 2014.

claim: Infection with a blasticidin-selectable HCV genome in immortalized Stat1 knockout MEFs expressing human HCV entry factors, miR-122 and mApoE results in strong replication and particle production.
source: The only instance of viral infection in murine cells where strong replication and particle production were demonstrated relied on the use of a blasticidin-selectable genome (Jc1-bsd) in immortalized Stat1 knockout MEFs (iMEFs) expressing the human HCV entry factors, miR-122 and mApoE (Vogt et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vogt et al., 2013.

claim: The phenotypes of the triple CypA mutants in a murine context are the reverse of those observed in Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells.
source: The phenotypes of the triple mutants in this murine context were the reverse of those observed in Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells, suggesting that the mechanism by which these mutants function could depend to some extent on the species specificity of the cellular environment, which will be an interesting area for future study.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The mechanism by which CypA triple mutants function could depend on the species specificity of the cellular environment.
source: The phenotypes of the triple mutants in this murine context were the reverse of those observed in Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells, suggesting that the mechanism by which these mutants function could depend to some extent on the species specificity of the cellular environment, which will be an interesting area for future study.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed differences in phenotypes between human and murine contexts.

claim: More viral replication may be required to overcome an inhibitory effect of a murine factor on particle release.
source: Furthermore, if there is (a) murine factor(s) that is having an inhibitory effect on particle release, as observed for murine tetherin's block of HIV-1 particle release due to its resistance to Vpu-mediated degradation (McNatt et al., 2009), more viral replication may be required to overcome this.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: The luciferase assay used is extremely sensitive, capturing even low levels of replication that may be insufficient for robust infectious particle production.
source: The luciferase assay we used is extremely sensitive, capturing even low levels of replication that may simply be insufficient for robust infectious particle production.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sensitivity of the assay and the observed results.

claim: Other co-factors/adaptors may be necessary to facilitate CypA interactions and are missing or incompatible in murine cells.
source: To enhance replication, other (co-)factors/adaptors may be necessary to facilitate the interactions of CypA and are simply missing in murine cells or are incompatible orthologs of such factors.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: The effects of CypA observed in hepatoma lines may differ in a primary hepatocyte context and/or with the use of patient HCV isolates.
source: As observed for PI4KA, it is also possible that the effects of CypA we observe in the hepatoma lines tested may differ in a primary hepatocyte context and/or with the use of patient HCV isolates (Harak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Harak et al., 2017.

claim: Transduction efficiency of CypA ortholog constructs in Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells was >60%.
source: The percentage of GFP+ cells as determined by flow cytometry indicated >60% transduction efficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: All CypA orthologs were readily detected at the expected size of ~17 kDa by western blot except for squirrel monkey and pigtailed macaque CypA.
source: All the orthologs were readily detected at the expected size of ~17 kDa except for squirrel monkey CypA, the signal for which was <2 times that of the background levels in the nontransduced Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells, and pigtailed macaque CypA.
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The TRIM5-CypA fusion protein from pigtailed macaque was expected at ~51 kDa but no signal was observed with either antibody.
source: In the latter case, the TRIM5-CypA fusion protein was expected at ~51 kDa but no signal was observed with either antibody.
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Expression of human CypA in Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells increased HCV replication by more than two logs relative to non-rescued cells at five days post-infection.
source: As expected, expression of human CypA in Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells increased HCV replication by more than two logs relative to the non-rescued cells at five days post-infection (dpi) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The lack of HCV replication in cells transduced with squirrel monkey and pigtailed macaque CypA may be due to these proteins not being properly expressed.
source: It remains possible that the lack of HCV replication in cells transduced with squirrel monkey and pigtailed macaque CypA is due to these proteins not being properly expressed.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential explanations for the observed results.

claim: It is more likely that the antibody reactivity for squirrel monkey and pigtailed macaque CypA is weaker than that these proteins are not expressed.
source: However, as the transduction efficiency of our constructs expressing pigtailed macaque and squirrel monkey CypA was robust and we were able to detect all other CypA variants utilized in this study by western blot, it is more likely that the antibody reactivity for these two specific orthologs is weaker.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transduction efficiency and detection of other CypA variants.

claim: Mutating residue 52 in the triple mutant T11A/A12V/D14G did not have a significant synergistic effect on HCV replication.
source: Mutating residue 52, even in the triple mutant, did not have a significant synergistic effect for any of the mutants tested (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The number of NS5A positive cells in the mouse CypA rescue line was significantly higher than that of the non-transduced Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells.
source: Although significantly less compared to these two lines, the number of NS5A positive cells in the mouse rescue line was still significantly higher than that of the non-transduced Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Supernatants collected from parental Huh7.5 shRNA CypA cells did not exhibit an increase in infectious particles over time.
source: Supernatants collected from parental Huh7.5 shRNA CypA cells did not exhibit an increase in infectious particles over time, as replication levels in Huh7.5 cells did not significantly increase following infection with the five dpi supernatant.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: There was still some infectious particle production in parental Huh7.5 shRNA CypA cells as the level of replication was at least a log above background.
source: However, there clearly was still some infectious particle production occurring as the level of replication was at least a log above background.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Replication was consistently highest in Huh7 cells compared to Clone 8 cells.
source: Replication was consistently highest in the Huh7 cells, with the difference between the Clone 8/Clone 8 + ApoE and Huh7 cells increasing over time till by six dpi there was an approximately three-log difference in luciferase activity.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The levels of replication in the parental Hep56.1D cells traced that of mock, with no de novo replication observed after the first wash of cells at two dpi.
source: The levels of replication in the parental Hep56.1D cells traced that of mock, with no de novo replication observed after the first wash of cells at two dpi.
